title: حِكَايَةُ الْمَلِكِ عُمَرَ بْنِ النُّعْمَانِ
part: Night 141 · King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān, continued
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 674–678 (Night 141, continuing directly from nights-140), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 141 continues the tale of King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān. The dying horse-thief finishes his story: Kahrdāsh took the horse from the old woman Dhāt al-Dawāhī, she talked him into letting her go, and the thief followed the robbers, stole the horse and fought his way out wounded. Kān Mā Kān tells him who he is; the thief recites verses repenting a life of horse-stealing, bequeaths him the horse al-Qātūl, and dies, and Kān Mā Kān buries him. Meanwhile the vizier Dandān has broken with King Sāsān, taken half the army and sworn to put Kān Mā Kān on the throne. Kān Mā Kān rides back to Baghdad, where Sāsān, fearing Dandān, receives him with honour, gifts and the largest apartments in the palace. His mother will not carry his suit to his cousin Qaḍā Fakān, so he turns to an old go-between, Saʿdāna, who comes back saying the cousin will visit him at midnight. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ الْحَادِيَةُ وَالْأَرْبَعُونَ بَعْدَ الْمِائَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-ḥādiyatu wa-al-arbaʿūna baʿda al-miʾati
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the first-and-forty after the hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the hundred and forty-first night,
sentences.n: al-ḥādiya, “the first”, is the ordinal used for “one” inside a compound number; it is feminine to agree with layla. al-arbaʿūn, “forty”, keeps its cardinal form and is joined by wa-.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُ أَنَّ الْفَارِسَ الْمَجْرُوحَ قَالَ لِكَانَ مَا كَانَ فَخَرَجَ عَلَى الْعَجُوزِ وَمَنْ مَعَهَا كَهْرْدَاشُ وَأَطْبَقَ عَلَيْهِمْ وَصَاحَ بِهِمْ وَهَاشَ
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna al-fārisa al-majrūḥa qāla li-kāna mā kāna fa-kharaja ʿalā al-ʿajūzi wa-man maʿahā kahrdāshu wa-aṭbaqa ʿalayhim wa-ṣāḥa bihim wa-hāsha
sentences.l: She said: It has reached me, O king the happy, that the horseman, the wounded-one, said to Kān Mā Kān: And Kahrdāsh came out upon the old-woman and whoever (was) with her, and closed-in upon them, and shouted at them, and stormed.
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that the wounded horseman went on to Kān Mā Kān: “Kahrdāsh fell upon the old woman and her company, closed in on them on every side, shouted at them and stormed at them.
sentences.n: kharaja ʿalā, “to come out against”, to sally out at someone. The subject kahrdāsh comes after the prepositional phrase, at the end of its clause. aṭbaqa ʿalā, “to close down upon”, to surround completely. ṣāḥa bi-, “to shout at”. hāsha is the least certain word here: it means “to be in an uproar, rush about in commotion”, and is read so here, “and stormed”; treat the exact sense as a guess.

sentences.t: وَمَا كَانَ إِلَّا سَاعَةٌ حَتَّى رَبَطَ الْعَشَرَةَ عَبِيدٍ وَالْعَجُوزَ وَتَسَلَّمَ مِنْهُمُ الْحِصَانَ وَسَارَ بِهِمْ فَرْحَانَ
sentences.tr: wa-mā kāna illā sāʿatun ḥattā rabaṭa al-ʿasharata ʿabīdin wa-al-ʿajūza wa-tasallama minhumu al-ḥiṣāna wa-sāra bihim farḥāna
sentences.l: And there was not but an hour until he bound the ten slaves and the old-woman, and took-over from them the horse, and went-off with them, glad.
sentences.i: In no more than an hour he had bound the ten slaves and the old woman, taken the horse from them, and ridden off with them, well pleased.
sentences.n: mā kāna illā sāʿatun ḥattā, “there was only an hour before”, a stock way of saying how fast something happened; kāna here simply means “there was”. al-ʿashara ʿabīd, “the ten slaves”: Classical would say al-ʿabīd al-ʿashara or ʿasharat al-ʿabīd; putting the article on the number and leaving the noun bare is Middle Arabic. tasallama, “to take delivery of, take possession of”; the print marks its doubled lām. farḥān, “glad”, describes his state as he rides off.

sentences.t: فَقُلْتُ فِي نَفْسِي ضَاعَ تَعَبِي وَمَا بَلَغْتُ أَرَبِي
sentences.tr: fa-qultu fī nafsī ḍāʿa taʿabī wa-mā balaghtu arabī
sentences.l: And I said in my soul: My toil is lost, and I did not attain my aim.
sentences.i: I said to myself, ‘All my trouble has gone for nothing, and I have not got what I came for.’
sentences.n: qāla fī nafsihi, “to say to oneself”. ḍāʿa, “to be lost, go to waste”. arab, “need, aim, object”. Rhyme: taʿabī / arabī.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ صَبَرْتُ حَتَّى أَنْظُرَ مَا يَؤُلُ إِلَيْهِ الْأَمْرُ
sentences.tr: thumma ṣabartu ḥattā anẓura mā yaʾūlu ilayhi al-amru
sentences.l: Then I was-patient until I should see what the matter would come-round to.
sentences.i: Then I bided my time, to see how matters would turn out.
sentences.n: ḥattā with the subjunctive anẓura, “so that I might see”. āla ilā, “to come in the end to, result in”; its imperfect is yaʾūlu, which the print spells with a single wāw (يؤل), a common short spelling, kept here.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَأَتِ الْعَجُوزُ نَفْسَهَا فِى الْأَسْرِ بَكَتْ وَقَالَتْ لِلْمُقَدَّمِ كَهْرْدَاشَ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾati al-ʿajūzu nafsahā fī al-asri bakat wa-qālat li-al-muqaddami kahrdāsha
sentences.l: And when the old-woman saw herself in the captivity, she wept and said to the leader Kahrdāsh:
sentences.i: When the old woman saw that she was a prisoner, she wept and said to the chief, Kahrdāsh,
sentences.n: raʾā nafsahu fī, “to see oneself in”, to find oneself in a plight. asr, “captivity”. muqaddam, “leader” of a band, as at the end of the last night; Kahrdāsh stands in apposition to it.

sentences.t: أَيُّهَا الْفَارِسُ الْهُمَامُ وَالْبَطَلُ الضِّرْغَامُ مَاذَا تَصْنَعُ بِالْعَجُوزِ وَالْعَبِيدِ وَقَدْ بَلَغْتَ مِنَ الْحِصَانِ مَا تُرِيدُ
sentences.tr: ayyuhā al-fārisu al-humāmu wa-al-baṭalu al-ḍirghāmu mādhā taṣnaʿu bi-al-ʿajūzi wa-al-ʿabīdi wa-qad balaghta mina al-ḥiṣāni mā turīdu
sentences.l: O horseman, the valiant, and champion, the lion-like: what will you do with the old-woman and the slaves, when you have attained from the horse what you want?
sentences.i: ‘O valiant horseman, O lion-hearted champion, what will you do with an old woman and some slaves, now that you have the horse you wanted?’
sentences.n: Her flattery is sajʿ: humām / ḍirghām, then ʿabīd / turīd. humām, “high-minded hero”; ḍirghām, “lion”, used as an epithet, “fierce as a lion”. ṣanaʿa bi-, “to do with, deal with”. wa-qad balaghta, “when you have already attained”: wa- with qad and a perfect makes a circumstantial clause. balagha min … mā, “to get of … what”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّهَا خَادَعَتْهُ بِلِينِ الْكَلَامِ وَحَلَفَتْ أَنَّهَا تَسُوقُ لَهُ الْخَيْلَ وَالْأَنْعَامَ فَأَطْلَقَ الْعَبِيدَ وَأَطْلَقَهَا
sentences.tr: thumma innahā khādaʿathu bi-līni al-kalāmi wa-ḥalafat annahā tasūqu lahu al-khayla wa-al-anʿāma fa-aṭlaqa al-ʿabīda wa-aṭlaqahā
sentences.l: Then she beguiled him with softness of the speech, and swore that she would drive to him the horses and the cattle; so he released the slaves and released her.
sentences.i: Then she beguiled him with soft words, swearing that she would drive horses and cattle to him in payment, and he let the slaves go, and her with them.
sentences.n: thumma innahā, “then she”: innahā simply carries the new subject, a narrative habit of the Nights. khādaʿa, “to try to deceive, beguile”. bi-līn al-kalām, “with softness of speech”. sāqa, “to drive” animals; anʿām, “livestock”, chiefly camels, cattle and sheep. Rhyme: al-kalām / al-anʿām.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ سَارَ هُوَ وَأَصْحَابُهُ وَتَبِعْتُهُمْ حَتَّى وَصَلُوا إِلَى هٰذِهِ الدِّيَارِ وَأَنَا أُلَاحِظُهُ وَأَتْبَعُهُ
sentences.tr: thumma sāra huwa wa-aṣḥābuhu wa-tabiʿtuhum ḥattā waṣalū ilā hādhihi al-diyāri wa-anā ulāḥiẓuhu wa-atbaʿuhu
sentences.l: Then he went-off, he and his companions, and I followed them until they reached these abodes, and I (was) keeping-an-eye on it and following it.
sentences.i: Then he rode on with his men, and I followed them until they came into these parts, all the while keeping my eye on the horse and dogging it.
sentences.n: sāra huwa wa-aṣḥābuhu: the pronoun huwa is needed before another subject can be joined to the one hidden in the verb. The print marks the damma of tabiʿtuhum. diyār, “abodes, lands”. lāḥaẓa, “to watch, keep in view”; its -hu, like that of atbaʿuhu, is the horse.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا وَجَدْتُ إِلَيْهِ سَبِيلًا سَرَقْتُهُ وَرَكِبْتُهُ وَأَخْرَجْتُ مِنْ مِخْلَاتِي سَوْطًا وَضَرَبْتُهُ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā wajadtu ilayhi sabīlan saraqtuhu wa-rakibtuhu wa-akhrajtu min mikhlātī sawṭan wa-ḍarabtuhu
sentences.l: And when I found to it a way, I stole it and mounted it, and brought-out from my nosebag a whip and struck it.
sentences.i: When at last I found my way to it, I stole it, mounted it, took a whip out of my saddlebag and lashed it on.
sentences.n: wajada ilayhi sabīlan, “to find a way to it”, an expression familiar from the Qurʾān (3:97, man istaṭāʿa ilayhi sabīlan, “whoever is able to find a way to it”). mikhlāh, “nosebag”, the feed bag a rider carries for his horse, here also his holdall.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا أَحَسُّوا بِي لَحِقُونِي وَأَحَاطُوا بِي مِنْ كُلِّ مَكَانٍ وَرَمَوْنِي بِالسِّهَامِ وَالسِّنَانِ وَأَنَا ثَابِتٌ عَلَيْهِ وَهُوَ يُقَاتِلُ عَنِّي بِيَدَيْهِ وَرِجْلَيْهِ إِلَى أَنْ أَخْرَجَ بِي مِنْ بَيْنِهِمْ مِثْلَ السَّهْمِ الرَّاشِقِ وَالنَّجْمِ الطَّارِقِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā aḥassū bī laḥiqūnī wa-aḥāṭū bī min kulli makānin wa-ramawnī bi-al-sihāmi wa-al-sināni wa-anā thābitun ʿalayhi wa-huwa yuqātilu ʿannī bi-yadayhi wa-rijlayhi ilā an akhraja bī min baynihim mithla al-sahmi al-rāshiqi wa-al-najmi al-ṭāriqi
sentences.l: And when they sensed me, they overtook me and surrounded me from every place, and pelted me with the arrows and the spear-point, and I (was) firm upon it, and it fighting for me with its hands and its feet, until it brought me out from among them like the arrow, the darting, and the star, the night-comer.
sentences.i: But they got wind of me, came up with me and surrounded me on every side, and showered me with arrows and spears; yet I kept my seat, and the horse fought for me with its forefeet and hind feet, until it carried me out from among them like a darting arrow or a shooting star.
sentences.n: aḥassa bi-, “to perceive, become aware of”; the print marks the doubled sīn. aḥāṭa bi-, “to surround”. ramā bi-, “to pelt with”: bi- marks the missiles. sinān, “spearhead”, singular for the whole volley. ʿan in yuqātilu ʿannī means “on my behalf”. The horse fights with its “hands and feet”, Arabic's usual words for a horse's fore and hind legs. akhraja bī, “brought me out”, sets bi- on a verb already causative; Classical would say akhrajanī or kharaja bī, so this doubling is a Middle Arabic touch, or perhaps a slip. al-ṭāriq, “the night-visitor”, is the star of Qurʾān 86:1–3. Rhyme: al-rāshiq / al-ṭāriq.

sentences.t: وَلٰكِنْ لَمَّا اشْتَدَّ الْكِفَاحُ أَصَابَنِي بَعْضُ الْجِرَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-lākin lammā ishtadda al-kifāḥu aṣābanī baʿḍu al-jirāḥi
sentences.l: But when the combat grew-fierce, some of the wounds struck me.
sentences.i: But when the fighting was at its fiercest I took some wounds.
sentences.n: kifāḥ, “hand-to-hand combat”. jirāḥ, plural of jurḥ, “wound”. Rhyme: al-kifāḥ / al-jirāḥ.

sentences.t: وَقَدْ مَضَى لِي عَلَى ظَهْرِهِ ثَلٰثَةُ أَيَّامٍ لَمْ أَذُقْ مَنَامًا وَلَا أَلْتَذَّ بِطَعَامٍ وَقَدْ ضَعُفَتْ مِنِّى الْقُوَى وَهَانَتْ عَلَيَّ الدُّنْيَا
sentences.tr: wa-qad maḍā lī ʿalā ẓahrihi thalāthatu ayyāmin lam adhuq manāman wa-lā altadhdha bi-ṭaʿāmin wa-qad ḍaʿufat minnī al-quwā wa-hānat ʿalayya al-dunyā
sentences.l: And there have passed for me on its back three days, I have not tasted a sleep, nor taken-pleasure in a food; and the strengths have weakened from me, and the world has become-cheap upon me.
sentences.i: I have now been three days on its back without tasting sleep or relishing a mouthful of food; my strength has failed me, and the world has grown of little worth to me.
sentences.n: maḍā lī … thalāthatu ayyām, “three days have passed for me”, the usual way to say how long one has been doing something. The print spells thalātha with a dagger alif (ثلٰثة). lam governs both verbs: adhuq and altadhdha are jussive, the second carried on by wa-lā. dhāqa al-manām, “to taste sleep”. Rhyme: manām / ṭaʿām. quwā, plural of quwwa, “powers, strength”. hāna ʿalā, “to be of little account to”: life no longer matters to him. The print marks the shadda of ʿalayya.

sentences.t: وَأَنْتَ أَحْسَنْتَ إِلَيَّ وَشَفِقْتَ عَلَيَّ وَأَرَاكَ عَارِىَ الْجَسَدِ ظَاهِرَ الْكَمَدِ وَيَلُوحُ عَلَيْكَ أَثَرُ النِّعْمَةِ
sentences.tr: wa-anta aḥsanta ilayya wa-shafiqta ʿalayya wa-arāka ʿāriya al-jasadi ẓāhira al-kamadi wa-yalūḥu ʿalayka atharu al-niʿmati
sentences.l: And you have done-good to me and have taken-pity on me; and I see you bare of the body, apparent of the grief, and there shines upon you the trace of the prosperity.
sentences.i: You have been kind to me and taken pity on me. I see you with your body bare and your grief plain to see, and yet the marks of good fortune show upon you.
sentences.n: aḥsana ilā, “to do good to”. shafiqa ʿalā, “to pity, feel tender concern for”; the usual form is ashfaqa ʿalā, but the simple verb is also found. ʿāriya al-jasad, ẓāhira al-kamad, “bare of body, plain of grief”: each adjective describes “you” and is followed by a noun saying in what respect, a compact construction (iḍāfa of an adjective). The print writes ʿārī with final ى. kamad, “hidden sorrow, heartache”. Rhyme: al-jasad / al-kamad. athar al-niʿma, “the trace of ease”, the look of someone raised in comfort.

sentences.t: فَمَنْ أَنْتَ وَمِنْ أَيْنَ أَقْبَلْتَ وَإِلَى أَيْنَ تُرِيدُ
sentences.tr: fa-man anta wa-min ayna aqbalta wa-ilā ayna turīdu
sentences.l: So who (are) you, and from where have you come, and to where do you want (to go)?
sentences.i: So who are you, where have you come from, and where are you bound?”
sentences.n: ilā ayna turīdu, “where do you want (to go)?”: arāda ilā, with the verb of motion understood, is the ordinary way to ask a traveller's destination.

sentences.t: فَقُلْتُ لَهُ أَنَا اسْمِي كَانَ مَا كَانَ ابْنُ الْمَلِكِ ضَوْءِ الْمَكَانِ ابْنِ الْمَلِكِ عُمَرَ بْنِ النُّعْمَانِ
sentences.tr: fa-qultu lahu anā ismī kāna mā kāna ibnu al-maliki ḍawʾi al-makāni ibni al-maliki ʿumara bni al-nuʿmāni
sentences.l: And I said to him: I, my name (is) Kān Mā Kān, son of King Ḍawʾ al-Makān, son of King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān.
sentences.i: And I said to him, “My name is Kān Mā Kān, son of King Ḍawʾ al-Makān, son of King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān.
sentences.n: fa-qultu, “and I said”: the narrative slips into the first person, as though Kān Mā Kān were telling his own story, and goes back to the third person a few lines on (ḥaddathahu). anā ismī, “I, my name is”: the topic set first and taken up by the pronoun. Rhyme: al-makān / al-nuʿmān. The name Kān Mā Kān does not decline.

sentences.t: قَدْ مَاتَ وَالِدِى وَتَرَبَّيْتُ يَتِيمًا وَتَوَلَّى بَعْدَهُ رَجُلٌ لَئِيمٌ وَصَارَ مَلِكًا عَلَى الْحَقِيرِ وَالْعَظِيمِ
sentences.tr: qad māta wālidī wa-tarabbaytu yatīman wa-tawallā baʿdahu rajulun laʾīmun wa-ṣāra malikan ʿalā al-ḥaqīri wa-al-ʿaẓīmi
sentences.l: My father has died, and I grew-up an orphan, and there took-charge after him a man, base, and he became king over the lowly and the great.
sentences.i: My father is dead, and I grew up an orphan; after him a base man seized the throne and became king over high and low alike.”
sentences.n: tarabbā, “to be brought up, grow up”. tawallā, “to take office, assume rule”; the print marks its doubled lām. laʾīm, “base, ignoble”, means King Sāsān. al-ḥaqīr wa-al-ʿaẓīm, “the lowly and the great”, that is, everyone. Rhyme: yatīm / laʾīm / al-ʿaẓīm.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ حَدَّثَهُ بِحَدِيثِهِ مِنْ أَوَّلِهِ إِلَى آخِرِهِ
sentences.tr: thumma ḥaddathahu bi-ḥadīthihi min awwalihi ilā ākhirihi
sentences.l: Then he told him his story from its first to its last.
sentences.i: Then he told him his whole story from beginning to end.
sentences.n: ḥaddatha bi-, “to tell (someone) of”: the person told is the direct object, the thing told takes bi-. The print marks the doubled dāl and the doubled wāw of awwalihi. Here the narrative is in the third person again.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ السَّلَّالُ وَقَدْ رَقَّ لَهُ وَاللَّهِ إِنَّكَ ذُو حَسَبٍ عَظِيمٍ وَشَرَفٍ جَسِيمٍ وَسَيَكُونُ لَكَ شَأْنٌ وَتَصِيرُ أَفْرَسَ أَهْلِ هٰذَا الزَّمَانِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu al-sallālu wa-qad raqqa lahu wa-allāhi innaka dhū ḥasabin ʿaẓīmin wa-sharafin jasīmin wa-sa-yakūnu laka shaʾnun wa-taṣīru afrasa ahli hādhā al-zamāni
sentences.l: And the horse-thief said to him, and he had softened toward him: By God, you are possessor of a lineage, great, and a nobility, vast; and there will be for you a standing, and you will become the best-horseman of the people of this time.
sentences.i: The horse-thief, moved to pity for him, said, “By God, you come of a great house and a lofty nobility; you will be a man of mark, and the finest horseman of this age.
sentences.n: al-sallāl, “the horse-thief”, Ghassān's trade used as his name. raqqa li-, “to soften toward, feel for”. ḥasab, “inherited merit, lineage”. Rhyme: ʿaẓīm / jasīm, then shaʾn / al-zamān. The print spells shaʾn without hamza (شان). afras, “most skilled at horsemanship”, an elative from faras, “horse”.

sentences.t: فَإِنْ قَدَرْتَ أَنْ تَحْمِلَنِي وَأَنْتَ رَاكِبٌ وَرَائِي وَتُؤَدِّيَنِى إِلَى بِلَادِي يَكُنْ لَكَ الشَّرَفُ فِى الدُّنْيَا وَالْأَجْرُ فِي يَوْمِ التَّنَادِي
sentences.tr: fa-in qadarta an taḥmilanī wa-anta rākibun warāʾī wa-tuʾaddiyanī ilā bilādī yakun laka al-sharafu fī al-dunyā wa-al-ajru fī yawmi al-tanādī
sentences.l: So if you are-able to carry me, you riding behind me, and to deliver me to my land, there will be for you the honour in the world and the reward on the Day of the Calling-to-one-another.
sentences.i: If you can carry me, riding behind me, and bring me to my own country, you will have honour in this world and your reward on the Day of Mutual Calling.
sentences.n: The conditional in takes jussive yakun in the answer. taḥmilanī wa-tuʾaddiyanī share the subjunctive after an. wa-anta rākibun warāʾī, “with you riding behind me”: a circumstantial clause; the thief, too weak to keep his seat, wants Kān Mā Kān mounted behind him to hold him on. addā ilā, “to bring, deliver to”. yawm al-tanādī, “the Day of Calling to One Another”, a name for the Day of Judgement from Qurʾān 40:32, where the Qurʾān spells it al-tanād. Rhyme: bilādī / al-tanādī.

sentences.t: فَإِنَّهُ مَا بَقِيَ لِي قُوَّةٌ أُمْسِكُ بِهَا نَفْسِي وَإِنْ كَانَتِ الْأُخْرَى فَأَنْتَ بِالْجَوَادِ أَوْلَى مِنْ غَيْرِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-innahu mā baqiya lī quwwatun umsiku bihā nafsī wa-in kānati al-ukhrā fa-anta bi-al-jawādi awlā min ghayrika
sentences.l: For indeed there remains not to me a strength I may hold with it myself; and if it is the other, then you are more-entitled to the steed than other-than-you.
sentences.i: For I have no strength left to hold myself in the saddle; and if it should be the other thing, then the horse is yours by better right than anyone's.”
sentences.n: fa-innahu, “for it is that”: the pronoun -hu looks forward to the whole clause. baqiya is masculine though quwwa is feminine; agreement with a following feminine subject is often loose. amsaka nafsahu, “to hold oneself up, keep one's seat”. wa-in kānati al-ukhrā, “and if it is the other”, a euphemism: if I die. awlā bi-, “more entitled to, with a better claim to”.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ كَانَ مَا كَانَ وَاللَّهِ لَوْ قَدَرْتُ أَحْمِلُكَ عَلَي أَكْتَافِي أَوْ أُقَاسِمُكَ عُمْرِي لَفَعَلْتُ مِنْ غَيْرِ هٰذَا الْجَوَادِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu kāna mā kāna wa-allāhi law qadartu aḥmiluka ʿalā aktāfī aw uqāsimuka ʿumrī la-faʿaltu min ghayri hādhā al-jawādi
sentences.l: And Kān Mā Kān said to him: By God, if I were-able (to) carry you on my shoulders or share-with-you my lifetime, I would-have-done (it), without this steed.
sentences.i: Kān Mā Kān answered him, “By God, if I could carry you on my shoulders, or give you half of my own life, I would do it, and without any thought of this horse.
sentences.n: law qadartu aḥmiluka, “if I could carry you”: the second verb follows qadara with no an, the Middle Arabic shape met before (lā aqdiru aṣilu). la-faʿaltu, with la-, answers the law: “I would have done it.” qāsama, “to share with someone, go halves”. min ghayri, “without”: he wants no payment, horse or otherwise. The print writes ʿalā with a dotted yāʾ (علي).

sentences.t: لِأَنِّي مِنْ أَهْلِ الْمَعْرُوفِ وَإِغَاثَةِ الْمَلْهُوفِ وَفِعْلُ الْخَيْرِ لِوَجْهِ اللَّهِ تَعَالَى يَدْفَعُ سَبْعِينَ بَلَاءً عَنْ صَاحِبِهِ فَاعْزِمْ عَلَى الْمَسِيرِ وَتَوَكَّلْ عَلَى اللَّطِيفِ الْخَبِيرِ
sentences.tr: li-annī min ahli al-maʿrūfi wa-ighāthati al-malhūfi wa-fiʿlu al-khayri li-wajhi allāhi taʿālā yadfaʿu sabʿīna balāʾan ʿan ṣāḥibihi fa-iʿzim ʿalā al-masīri wa-tawakkal ʿalā al-laṭīfi al-khabīri
sentences.l: Because I (am) of the people of the kindness and the succouring of the distressed-one; and the doing of the good for the face of God, (may He be) exalted, repels seventy afflictions from its owner. So resolve on the journeying, and rely on the Gentle, the All-Aware.
sentences.i: For I am one of those who do kindness and come to the help of the distressed, and a good deed done for God’s sake alone wards off seventy calamities from the one who does it. So make up your mind to the journey, and put your trust in the Gentle, the All-Aware.”
sentences.n: Rhyme: maʿrūf, malhūf; then masīr, khabīr. ahl al-maʿrūf, “people of kindness”, the generous. malhūf, “one in distress, crying for help”. li-wajhi Allāh, “for the face of God”, that is, for God’s sake and nothing else. ṣāḥib, “owner, companion”, here the doer of the deed. tawakkala ʿalā, “to put one’s trust in”. al-Laṭīf al-Khabīr, “the Subtle, the All-Aware”, are two of God’s names, paired so in the Qurʾān (6:103, 67:14).

sentences.t: فَأَرَادَ أَنْ يَحْمِلَهُ عَلَى الْحِصَانِ وَيَسِيرَ مُتَوَكِّلًا عَلَى اللَّهِ الْمُسْتَعَانِ
sentences.tr: fa-arāda an yaḥmilahu ʿalā al-ḥiṣāni wa-yasīra mutawakkilan ʿalā allāhi al-mustaʿāni
sentences.l: And he wanted to lift him onto the horse and go, relying on God, the One-whose-help-is-sought.
sentences.i: He made to lift him onto the horse and set off, trusting in God, whose help is sought.
sentences.n: Rhyme: ḥiṣān, mustaʿān. al-mustaʿān, “the one whose aid is asked”, comes from the Qurʾān (12:18, wa-Allāhu al-mustaʿān).

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ اصْبِرْ عَلَيَّ قَلِيلًا
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu iṣbir ʿalayya qalīlan
sentences.l: And he said to him: Be-patient with me a little.
sentences.i: But the man said to him, “Wait a little for me.”
sentences.n: ṣabara ʿalā, “to be patient with, bear with” someone; the print marks the doubled yāʾ of ʿalayya.

sentences.t: فَغَمَّضَ عَيْنَيْهِ وَفَتَحَ يَدَيْهِ وَقَالَ أَشْهَدُ أَنْ لَا إِلٰهَ إِلَّا اللَّهُ وَأَشْهَدُ أَنَّ مُحَمَّدًا رَسُولُ اللَّهِ
sentences.tr: fa-ghammaḍa ʿaynayhi wa-fataḥa yadayhi wa-qāla ashhadu an lā ilāha illā allāhu wa-ashhadu anna muḥammadan rasūlu allāhi
sentences.l: And he closed his two eyes and opened his two hands and said: I bear-witness that (there is) no god except God, and I bear-witness that Muḥammad (is) the messenger of God.
sentences.i: He closed his eyes, opened his hands, and said, “I bear witness that there is no god but God, and I bear witness that Muḥammad is the Messenger of God.”
sentences.n: The shahāda, the profession of faith, said by the dying. ghammaḍa ʿaynayhi, “to shut one’s eyes”. Opening the hands, palms up, is the posture of prayer.

sentences.t: وَقَالَ يَا عَظِيمُ اغْفِرْ لِيَ الذَّنْبَ الْعَظِيمَ فَإِنَّهُ لَا يَغْفِرُ الذَّنْبَ الْعَظِيمَ إِلَّا الْعَظِيمُ
sentences.tr: wa-qāla yā ʿaẓīmu ighfir liya al-dhanba al-ʿaẓīma fa-innahu lā yaghfiru al-dhanba al-ʿaẓīma illā al-ʿaẓīmu
sentences.l: And he said: O Mighty-One, forgive me the sin, the mighty; for indeed, none forgives the mighty sin except the Mighty-One.
sentences.i: Then he said, “O Mighty One, forgive me my mighty sin, for none forgives a mighty sin but the Mighty.”
sentences.n: A play on one word: ʿaẓīm is both God’s name “the Mighty” and the size of the sin. yā ʿaẓīmu takes a ḍamma with no tanwīn, as a vocative addressed to one person does. ghafara li-, “to forgive someone”: the person forgiven takes li-, the sin is the object.

sentences.t: وَتَهَيَّأَ لِلْمُهِمَّاتِ وَأَنْشَدَ هٰذِهِ الْأَبْيَاتَ
sentences.tr: wa-tahayyaʾa li-al-muhimmāti wa-anshada hādhihi al-abyāta
sentences.l: And he made-himself-ready for the weighty-matters and recited these verses:
sentences.i: And he made himself ready for what lay before him, and recited these verses:
sentences.n: tahayyaʾa li-, “to get ready for”; the print marks the doubled yāʾ. muhimmāt, “grave matters, things of moment”, here death itself. Rhyme: muhimmāt, abyāt.

sentences.t:
ظَلَمْتُ الْعِبَادَ وَطُفْتُ الْبِلَادَ * وَأَمْضَيْتُ عُمْرِي بِشُرْبِ الْخُمُوْر
وَخُضْتُ السُّيُوْلَ لِسَلِّ الْخُيُوْلِ * وَهَدْمِ الطُّلُوْلِ بِفِعْلِ النَّكُوْر
وَأَمْرِي عَظِيْمٌ وَجُرْمِي جَسِيْم * وَقَاتُوْلُ مِنِيْ تَمَامُ الْاُمُوْر
وَاَمَّلْتُ اِنِّي اَنَالُ الْمُنَى * بِذَاكَ الْحِصَانِ فَاَعْيَى مَسِيرِي
وَطُوْلُ الْحَيٰوةِ اَسُلُّ الْخُيُوْلَ * فَكَانَتْ وَفَاتِي عِنْدَ الْقَدِيْر
وَآخِرُ اَمْرِيَ اِنِّي تَعِبْتُ * لِرِزْقِ الْغَرِيْبِ الْيَتِيْمِ الْفَقِيْر
sentences.tr:
ẓalamtu al-ʿibāda wa-ṭuftu al-bilād * wa-amḍaytu ʿumrī bi-shurbi al-khumūr
wa-khuḍtu al-suyūla li-salli al-khuyūli * wa-hadmi al-ṭulūli bi-fiʿli al-nakūr
wa-amrī ʿaẓīmun wa-jurmī jasīm * wa-qātūlu minī tamāmu al-umūr
wa-ammaltu innī anālu al-munā * bi-dhāka al-ḥiṣāni fa-aʿyā masīrī
wa-ṭūlu al-ḥayāti asullu al-khuyūla * fa-kānat wafātī ʿinda al-qadīr
wa-ākhiru amriya innī taʿibtu * li-rizqi al-gharībi al-yatīmi al-faqīr
sentences.n: Metre mutaqārib (faʿūlun four times in each half-line). The rhyme letter is rāʾ, and the vowel before it swings between ū (khumūr, nakūr, umūr) and ī (masīrī, qadīr, faqīr), which the rules of rhyme allow. The print points every word; the pointing is kept as it stands, including the sukūn it sets on long ū and ī (الْخُمُوْر, جَسِيْم). ṭulūl, “traces of abandoned dwellings”, here homes left in ruins. al-nakūr, “the abominable”, an intensive form. The third line is doubtful: the print has مِنِيْ, which most likely stands for minnī, “from me, on my part”, with the doubling unmarked, so that Qātūl is the last and greatest of his deeds; a reading munā(ya), “my desire”, is possible but does not suit the pointing. The fourth line has اَعْيَى, aʿyā, “to be worn out, fail”. In the last line he means Kān Mā Kān: the horse he toiled for will now feed a fatherless exile. ḥayāt is written with the old spelling and a dagger alif (الْحَيٰوة). The print points ṭūlu in the nominative where the sense, “all my life long”, would want the adverbial accusative ṭūla; the printed vowel is kept.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا فَرَغَ مِنْ شِعْرِهِ غَمَّضَ عَيْنَيْهِ وَفَتَحَ فَاهُ وَشَهَقَ شَهْقَةً فَفَارَقَ الدُّنْيَا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā faragha min shiʿrihi ghammaḍa ʿaynayhi wa-fataḥa fāhu wa-shahaqa shahqatan fa-fāraqa al-dunyā
sentences.l: And when he finished from his poetry, he closed his two eyes and opened his mouth and gasped a gasp, and departed-from the world.
sentences.i: When he had finished his poem, he closed his eyes, opened his mouth, gave one great gasp, and left this world.
sentences.n: faragha min, “to finish with”. fāhu, “his mouth”: fam takes this long form, fū, fā, fī, before a suffix. shahaqa shahqatan, verb with its own noun, “gave a gasp”. fāraqa al-dunyā, “to part from the world”, to die.

sentences.t: فَقَامَ كَانَ مَا كَانَ وَحَفَرَ لَهُ حُفْرَةً وَوَارَاهُ فِى التُّرَابِ ثُمَّ أَتَى إِلَى الْجَوَادِ فَقَبَّلَهُ وَمَسَحَ وَجْهَهُ وَفَرِحَ فَرَحًا شَدِيدًا وَقَالَ مَا أَحَدٌ حَظِيَ بِمِثْلِ هٰذَا الْحِصَانِ وَلَا هُوَ عِنْدَ الْمَلِكِ سَاسَانَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāma kāna mā kāna wa-ḥafara lahu ḥufratan wa-wārāhu fī al-turābi thumma atā ilā al-jawādi fa-qabbalahu wa-masaḥa wajhahu wa-fariḥa faraḥan shadīdan wa-qāla mā aḥadun ḥaẓiya bi-mithli hādhā al-ḥiṣāni wa-lā huwa ʿinda al-maliki sāsāna
sentences.l: And Kān Mā Kān rose and dug for him a pit and hid-him in the earth; then he came to the steed and kissed it and wiped its face, and rejoiced a rejoicing intense, and said: Not anyone has-been-favoured with the like of this horse, and not (even) is it with King Sāsān.
sentences.i: Kān Mā Kān rose, dug a grave for him and laid him in the earth. Then he went to the horse, kissed it, stroked its face, and was overjoyed, and said, “No one has ever been granted a horse like this one; not even King Sāsān has its equal.”
sentences.n: wārā, “to hide, cover over”, the usual word for burying the dead. fariḥa faraḥan shadīdan, verb with its own noun, “rejoiced greatly”. ḥaẓiya bi-, “to be granted, enjoy the good fortune of”. Rhyme: ḥiṣān, Sāsān.

sentences.t: هٰذَا مَا جَرَى لِكَانَ مَا كَانَ
sentences.tr: hādhā mā jarā li-kāna mā kāna
sentences.l: This (is) what happened to Kān Mā Kān.
sentences.i: So much for Kān Mā Kān.
sentences.n: jarā li-, “to befall”. The storyteller’s formula for leaving one thread and picking up another.

sentences.t: وَأَمَّا مَا كَانَ مِنْ أَمْرِ الْمَلِكِ سَاسَانَ فَإِنَّهُ أَتَتْهُ الْأَخْبَارُ أَنَّ الْوَزِيرَ دَنْدَانَ خَرَجَ عَنْ طَاعَةِ الْمَلِكِ سَاسَانَ هُوَ وَنِصْفُ الْعَسْكَرِ وَحَلَفُوا أَنْ مَالَهُمْ مَلِكٌ غَيْرُ كَانَ مَا كَانَ
sentences.tr: wa-ammā mā kāna min amri al-maliki sāsāna fa-innahu atathu al-akhbāru anna al-wazīra dandāna kharaja ʿan ṭāʿati al-maliki sāsāna huwa wa-niṣfu al-ʿaskari wa-ḥalafū an mā lahum malikun ghayru kāna mā kāna
sentences.l: And as for what was of the affair of King Sāsān, (it was) that the reports came to him that the vizier Dandān had gone-out from the obedience of King Sāsān, he and half the army, and they swore that (there is) not for them a king other-than Kān Mā Kān.
sentences.i: As for King Sāsān, word reached him that the vizier Dandān had thrown off his allegiance, he and half the army with him, and that they had sworn they would have no king but Kān Mā Kān.
sentences.n: wa-ammā mā kāna min amri X fa-…, “as for what befell X”: the matching formula that opens the new thread, with fa- introducing the main clause. kharaja ʿan ṭāʿati, “to go out of the obedience of”, to rebel. huwa wa-niṣfu al-ʿaskar, “he and half the army”: the pronoun is repeated so that a second subject can be added. The print runs mā into lahum (مالهم): an mā lahum, “that they have no”; an here is the lightened anna.

sentences.t: وَاسْتَوْثَقَ الْوَزِيرُ مِنَ الْعَسْكَرِ بِالْعُهُودِ وَالْأَيْمَانِ وَدَخَلَ بِهِمْ إِلَى جَزَائِرِ الْهِنْدِ وَالْبَرْبَرِ وَبِلَادِ السُّودَانِ وَاجْتَمَعَ مَعَهُمْ عَسَاكِرُ مِثْلُ الْبَحْرِ الزَّاخِرِ لَا يُعْرَفُ لَهُمْ أَوَّلٌ مِنْ آخِرٍ
sentences.tr: wa-istawthaqa al-wazīru mina al-ʿaskari bi-al-ʿuhūdi wa-al-aymāni wa-dakhala bihim ilā jazāʾiri al-hindi wa-al-barbari wa-bilādi al-sūdāni wa-ijtamaʿa maʿahum ʿasākiru mithlu al-baḥri al-zākhiri lā yuʿrafu lahum awwalun min ākhirin
sentences.l: And the vizier made-sure of the army by the covenants and the oaths, and entered with them into the islands of al-Hind and al-Barbar and the lands of the Blacks, and there gathered with them armies like the sea, the swelling, (of which) is not known for them a first from a last.
sentences.i: The vizier bound the army to him with covenants and oaths, and led them away to the islands of India, the Berber country and the lands of the Sūdān; and armies gathered to him there like the swelling sea, so many that no one could tell their van from their rear.
sentences.n: istawthaqa min, “to make sure of, secure a pledge from”. aymān, plural of yamīn, “oath”. dakhala bi-, “to enter with, lead into”. al-Sūdān, “the Blacks”, the lands south of Egypt and the Sahara; the geography is the storyteller’s, not the map’s. ijtamaʿa, singular, comes before a plural subject (ʿasākir), as a verb that leads may. lā yuʿrafu lahum awwalun min ākhirin, “their first was not known from their last”, a stock phrase for a host too great to see across. Rhyme: aymān, Sūdān; zākhir, ākhir.

sentences.t: وَعَزَمَ الْوَزِيرُ أَنْ يَقْصِدَ بِهِمْ مَدِينَةَ بَغْدَادَ وَيَمْلِكَ تِلْكَ الْبِلَادَ وَيَقْتُلَ مَنْ خَالَفَهُ مِنَ الْعِبَادِ
sentences.tr: wa-ʿazama al-wazīru an yaqṣida bihim madīnata baghdāda wa-yamlika tilka al-bilāda wa-yaqtula man khālafahu mina al-ʿibādi
sentences.l: And the vizier resolved to make-for with them the city of Baghdad, and possess those lands, and kill whoever opposed him of the servants (of God).
sentences.i: And the vizier resolved to march with them on the city of Baghdad, make himself master of those lands, and put to death any man who stood against him.
sentences.n: ʿazama an, “to resolve to”. qaṣada bi-, “to make for, bringing someone along”. ʿibād, “servants (of God)”, that is, people. Rhyme: Baghdād, bilād, ʿibād.

sentences.t: وَأَقْسَمَ عَلَى أَنَّهُ لَا يَرُدُّ سَيْفَ الْحَرْبِ إِلَى غِمْدِةِ حَتَّى يُمَلِّكَ كَانَ مَا كَانَ
sentences.tr: wa-aqsama ʿalā annahu lā yaruddu sayfa al-ḥarbi ilā ghimdihi ḥattā yumallika kāna mā kāna
sentences.l: And he swore that he would not return the sword of the war to its sheath until he makes-king Kān Mā Kān.
sentences.i: And he swore that he would not put the sword of war back in its sheath until he had made Kān Mā Kān king.
sentences.n: The subject is the vizier Dandān. aqsama ʿalā anna, “to swear that”: ʿalā marks what the oath binds him to, as with ḥalafa ʿalā. The print spells ghimdihi, “its sheath”, with tāʾ marbūṭa (غمدة) where the pronoun -hu (ه) is meant, a spelling habit of the edition, kept here. The print marks the shadda of yumallika, “he makes (someone) king”, the causative of malaka, “to rule”.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا بَلَغَتْهُ هٰذِةِ الْأَخْبَارُ غَرِقَ فِي بَحْرِ الْأَفْكَارِ وَعَلِمَ أَنَّ الدَّوْلَةَ انْحَرَفَتْ عَلَيْهِ الصِّغَارُ وَالْكِبَارُ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā balaghathu hādhihi al-akhbāru ghariqa fī baḥri al-afkāri wa-ʿalima anna al-dawlata inḥarafat ʿalayhi al-ṣighāru wa-al-kibāru
sentences.l: And when these reports reached him, he drowned in the sea of the thoughts, and knew that the state had turned-aside against him, the small and the great.
sentences.i: When this news reached King Sāsān, he was sunk in a sea of anxious thought, for he knew that the whole realm, high and low alike, had turned against him.
sentences.n: The “him” is King Sāsān. The print again writes hādhihi with tāʾ marbūṭa (هذة). Rhyme: afkār, kibār. inḥarafa ʿalā, “to swerve against, turn hostile to”. al-ṣighāru wa-al-kibāru, “the small and the great”, is the subject of inḥarafat; al-dawla is set at the head as the topic with no pronoun to take it up, a loose construction: the state, that is everyone in it from least to greatest, had turned against him.

sentences.t: فَزَادَ بِهِ الْغَمُّ وَكَثُرَ عَلَيْهِ الْهَمُّ وَفَتَحَ الْخَزَائِنَ وَفَرَّقَ عَلَى أَرْبَابِ دَوْلَتِهِ الْأَمْوَالَ
sentences.tr: fa-zāda bihi al-ghammu wa-kathura ʿalayhi al-hammu wa-fataḥa al-khazāʾina wa-farraqa ʿalā arbābi dawlatihi al-amwāla
sentences.l: And the grief increased with him, and the care grew-much upon him; and he opened the treasuries and distributed upon the lords of his state the moneys.
sentences.i: His grief grew and his cares multiplied; he opened the treasuries and lavished wealth on the great men of his realm.
sentences.n: Rhyme: ghamm, hamm — two near-synonyms for sorrow and worry, a favourite pairing. zāda bi-, “to grow heavy on”. farraqa ʿalā, “to distribute among”. arbāb al-dawla, “the lords of the state”, the grandees of the court.

sentences.t: وَتَمَنَّى أَنَّ كَانَ مَا كَانَ يَقْدَمُ عَلَيْهِ وَيَجْذِبُ قَلْبَهُ إِلَيْهِ بِالْمُلَاطَفَةِ وَالْإِحْسَانِ وَيَجْعَلُهُ أَمِيرًا عَلَى الْعَسَاكِرِ الَّذِينَ لَمْ يَزَالُوا تَحْتَ طَاعَتِهِ لِتَطْفَى بِهِ شَرَارَةُ جَمْرَتِهِ
sentences.tr: wa-tamannā anna kāna mā kāna yaqdamu ʿalayhi wa-yajdhibu qalbahu ilayhi bi-al-mulāṭafati wa-al-iḥsāni wa-yajʿaluhu amīran ʿalā al-ʿasākiri alladhīna lam yazālū taḥta ṭāʿatihi li-taṭfā bihi sharāratu jamratihi
sentences.l: And he wished that Kān Mā Kān would come to him, and (that) he would draw his heart to himself with the kindness and the beneficence, and make him commander over the troops who had not ceased (to be) under his obedience, so that through him the spark of his ember might be quenched.
sentences.i: And he longed for Kān Mā Kān to come back to him, so that he could win his heart with kindness and generosity and set him in command of the troops who were still loyal, and through him put out the sparks of this blaze.
sentences.n: qadima ʿalā, “to come to (someone), arrive at his court”. In wa-yajdhibu and wa-yajʿaluhu the subject shifts back to Sāsān: it is he who will win the young man over. lam yazālū, “they had not ceased”, here “they still remained”. li-taṭfā is printed with final yāʾ (لتطفى) for Classical li-taṭfaʾa, “that it be put out”: the hamza has dropped, as often in Middle Arabic. Whose “ember” (jamra) is meant is not clear: most likely the fire of Dandān's revolt; it could also be Sāsān's own burning distress.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ كَانَ مَا كَانَ لَمَّا بَلَغَهُ ذٰلِكَ الْخَبَرُ مِنَ التُّجَّارِ رَجَعَ مُسْرِعًا إِلَى بَغْدَادَ عَلَى ظَهْرِ ذٰلِكَ الْجَوَادِ
sentences.tr: thumma inna kāna mā kāna lammā balaghahu dhālika al-khabaru mina al-tujjāri rajaʿa musriʿan ilā baghdāda ʿalā ẓahri dhālika al-jawādi
sentences.l: Then (as for) Kān Mā Kān, when that news reached him from the merchants, he returned hastening to Baghdad on the back of that steed.
sentences.i: As for Kān Mā Kān, when he heard this news from the merchants, he rode back to Baghdad in haste on the back of that horse.
sentences.n: thumma inna, “then indeed”, is the storyteller's formula for turning to another character; the name that follows is the subject of inna, and the sentence it heads is picked up again by rajaʿa. musriʿan, “hastening”, an accusative of circumstance (ḥāl).

sentences.t: فَبَيْنَمَا الْمَلِكُ سَاسَانُ فِي أَرِيكَتِهِ حَيْرَانُ إِذْ سَمِعَ بِقُدُومِ كَانَ مَا كَانَ فَأَخْرَجَ جَمِيعَ الْعَسَاكِرِ وَوُجَهَاءَ بَغْدَادَ لِمُلَاقَاتِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-baynamā al-maliku sāsānu fī arīkatihi ḥayrānu idh samiʿa bi-qudūmi kāna mā kāna fa-akhraja jamīʿa al-ʿasākiri wa-wujahāʾa baghdāda li-mulāqātihi
sentences.l: And while King Sāsān (was) on his couch, bewildered, behold, he heard of the arrival of Kān Mā Kān; and he sent-out all the troops and the notables of Baghdad for the meeting of him.
sentences.i: While King Sāsān sat on his throne at his wits' end, word came to him that Kān Mā Kān had arrived, and he sent out the whole army and all the notables of Baghdad to meet him.
sentences.n: baynamā … idh, “while … suddenly”, the usual frame for an interruption. Rhyme: Sāsān, ḥayrān. arīka, “a couch, a raised seat”, here the royal divan. samiʿa bi-, “to hear of”. wujahāʾ, plural of wajīh, “notable, man of standing” (literally one who has a “face”, wajh).

sentences.t: فَخَرَجَ كُلُّ مَنْ فِي بَغْدَادَ وَلَاقَوْهُ وَمَشَوْا بَيْنَ يَدَيْهِ إِلَى الْقَصْرِ يُقَبِّلُونَ الْأَعْتَابَ
sentences.tr: fa-kharaja kullu man fī baghdāda wa-lāqawhu wa-mashaw bayna yadayhi ilā al-qaṣri yuqabbilūna al-aʿtāba
sentences.l: And everyone who (was) in Baghdad went out and met him, and walked between his two hands to the palace, kissing the thresholds.
sentences.i: Everyone in Baghdad came out and met him, and walked before him to the palace, kissing the ground at the thresholds.
sentences.n: kullu man takes a singular verb (kharaja), then the sentence slides into the plural (lāqawhu, mashaw), going by sense. bayna yadayhi, “between his two hands”, that is, in front of him, as an escort. aʿtāb, plural of ʿataba, “threshold”: kissing the threshold is a gesture of homage.

sentences.t: وَدَخَلَتِ الْجَوَارِي وَالطَّوَاشِيَّةُ إِلَى أُمِّهِ فَبَشَّرُوهَا بِقُدُومِهِ فَأَتَتْ إِلَيْهِ وَقَبَّلَتْهُ بَيْنَ عَيْنَيْهِ
sentences.tr: wa-dakhalati al-jawārī wa-al-ṭawāshiyyatu ilā ummihi fa-bashsharūhā bi-qudūmihi fa-atat ilayhi wa-qabbalathu bayna ʿaynayhi
sentences.l: And the slave-girls and the eunuchs went-in to his mother, and they gave-her-the-good-news of his arrival; and she came to him and kissed him between his eyes.
sentences.i: The slave-girls and the eunuchs went in to his mother with the good news of his arrival, and she came to him and kissed him on the forehead.
sentences.n: ṭawāshiyya, plural of ṭawāshī, “eunuch”, a word of the Mamluk period. bashshara bi-, “to bring someone good news of”; the masculine plural bashsharūhā covers the mixed group. atā ilā, “to come to”, where Classical usually says atāhu without a preposition. Kissing between the eyes is a mother's or elder's kiss of affection.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ يَا أُمَّاهْ دَعِينِي أَمْضِي إِلَى عَمِّي الْمَلِكِ سَاسَانَ الَّذِي غَمَرَنِي بِالنِّعْمَةِ وَالْإِحْسَانِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla yā ummāh daʿīnī amḍī ilā ʿammī al-maliki sāsāna alladhī ghamaranī bi-al-niʿmati wa-al-iḥsāni
sentences.l: And he said: O mother, let-me go to my uncle, King Sāsān, who overwhelmed me with the favour and the beneficence.
sentences.i: He said, “Mother, let me go first to my uncle King Sāsān, who has heaped favours and kindness upon me.”
sentences.n: yā ummāh, “O mother”, with the -āh of calling out. daʿīnī amḍī, “let me go”: Classical would have the jussive amḍi (or an amḍiya); the print's indicative amḍī with its yāʾ is the looser later usage. ʿammī, “my uncle”: Sāsān is in fact his aunt's husband, but ʿamm is used for any older kinsman by marriage, and the line is courtly rather than exact. Rhyme: Sāsān, iḥsān. ghamara bi-, “to flood, overwhelm with”.

sentences.t: هٰذَا وَقَدْ تَحَيَّرَتْ عُقُولُ أَهْلِ الْقَصْرِ وَالدَّوْلَةِ فِي حُسْنِ ذٰلِكَ الْحِصَانِ وَقَالُوا مَا مَلَكَ مِثْلَ هٰذَا إِنْسَانٌ
sentences.tr: hādhā wa-qad taḥayyarat ʿuqūlu ahli al-qaṣri wa-al-dawlati fī ḥusni dhālika al-ḥiṣāni wa-qālū mā malaka mithla hādhā insānun
sentences.l: This (was so); and the minds of the people of the palace and the state had been bewildered at the beauty of that horse, and they said: No human-being has owned the like of this.
sentences.i: Meanwhile everyone at the palace and the court was dazzled by the beauty of that horse, and they said, “No man has ever owned its equal.”
sentences.n: hādhā wa-, “this (being so), and …”, is a storyteller's link, roughly “meanwhile”. taḥayyara fī, “to be bewildered at”. Rhyme: ḥiṣān, insān. In mā malaka mithla hādhā insānun the subject insānun comes last, after the object, for the rhyme and for emphasis.

sentences.t: فَدَخَلَ كَانَ مَا كَانَ إِلَى الْمَلِكِ سَاسَانَ وَسَلَّمَ عَلَيْهِ فَقَامَ لَهُ فَقَبَّلَ كَانَ مَا كَانَ يَدَيْهِ وَرِجْلَيْهِ وَقَدَّمَ لَهُ الْحِصَانَ هَدِيَّةً
sentences.tr: fa-dakhala kāna mā kāna ilā al-maliki sāsāna wa-sallama ʿalayhi fa-qāma lahu fa-qabbala kāna mā kāna yadayhi wa-rijlayhi wa-qaddama lahu al-ḥiṣāna hadiyyatan
sentences.l: And Kān Mā Kān went-in to King Sāsān and greeted him, and he stood-up for him; and Kān Mā Kān kissed his two hands and his two feet, and presented to him the horse (as) a gift.
sentences.i: Kān Mā Kān went in to King Sāsān and greeted him, and the king rose to receive him; Kān Mā Kān kissed his hands and his feet and presented the horse to him as a gift.
sentences.n: sallama ʿalā, “to greet, say al-salāmu ʿalaykum to”. qāma lahu, “to rise for someone”, a mark of respect: here the king honours the young man. hadiyyatan, “as a gift”, an accusative of state or purpose.

sentences.t: فَرَحَّبَ بِهِ وَقَالَ لَهُ أَهْلًا وَسَهْلًا بِوَلَدِي كَانَ مَا كَانَ وَاللَّهِ لَقَدْ ضَاقَتْ بِي الدُّنْيَا لِغِيَابِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-raḥḥaba bihi wa-qāla lahu ahlan wa-sahlan bi-waladī kāna mā kāna wa-allāhi la-qad ḍāqat bī al-dunyā li-ghiyābika
sentences.l: And he welcomed him and said to him: Family and easy-ground to my son Kān Mā Kān! By God, the world had become narrow for me because of your absence,
sentences.i: He made him welcome and said, “Welcome, welcome, my son Kān Mā Kān! By God, the world has been too narrow for me while you were away,
sentences.n: raḥḥaba bi-, “to welcome”. ahlan wa-sahlan, literally “(you have come to) family and level ground”, the standing formula of welcome; bi- marks the person welcomed. la-qad with the perfect is emphatic, “truly has …”. ḍāqat bī al-dunyā, “the world grew narrow on me”, that is, I was in deep distress. li-, “because of”.

sentences.t: وَالْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ عَلَى سَلَامَتِكَ فَدَعَا لَهُ كَانَ مَا كَانَ
sentences.tr: wa-al-ḥamdu li-llāhi ʿalā salāmatika fa-daʿā lahu kāna mā kāna
sentences.l: and the praise (belongs) to God for your safety. And Kān Mā Kān prayed for him.
sentences.i: and praise be to God that you are safe and sound.” And Kān Mā Kān called down blessings on him.
sentences.n: al-ḥamdu li-llāh ʿalā salāmatika, “praise God for your safety”, is the usual greeting to someone back from a journey or out of danger; ʿalā gives the reason for the thanks. daʿā li-, “to pray for”, as against daʿā ʿalā, “to pray against, curse”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ نَظَرَ الْمَلِكُ إِلَى هٰذَا الْحِصَانِ الْمُسَمَّى بِالْقَاتُولِ فَعَرَفَ أَنَّهُ الْحِصَانُ الَّذِي كَانَ رَآهُ مِنْ سَنَةِ كَذَا وَكَذَا فِي حِصَارِ عَبَدَةِ الصُّلْبَانِ مَعَ أَبِيهِ ضَوْءِ الْمَكَانِ حِينَ قُتِلَ عَمُّهُ شَرْكَانُ وَقَالَ لَهُ لَوْقَدَرَ عَلَيْهِ أَبُوكَ لَاشْتَرَاهُ بِأَلْفِ جَوَادٍ
sentences.tr: thumma naẓara al-maliku ilā hādhā al-ḥiṣāni al-musammā bi-al-qātūli fa-ʿarafa annahu al-ḥiṣānu alladhī kāna raʾāhu min sanati kadhā wa-kadhā fī ḥiṣāri ʿabadati al-ṣulbāni maʿa abīhi ḍawʾi al-makāni ḥīna qutila ʿammuhu sharrukānu wa-qāla lahu law qadara ʿalayhi abūka la-ishtarāhu bi-alfi jawādin
sentences.l: Then the king looked at this horse, the one-named al-Qātūl, and he knew that it (was) the horse which he had seen it in the year such and such, at the siege of the worshippers of the crosses, with his father Ḍawʾ al-Makān, when his uncle Sharrukān was killed; and he said to him: If your father had been-able (to get) at it, he would-have-bought-it for a thousand steeds.
sentences.i: Then the king looked at this horse called al-Qātūl, and knew it for the horse he had seen years before, in such and such a year, at the siege of the Cross-worshippers, in company with the young man's father Ḍawʾ al-Makān, when his uncle Sharrukān was slain. And he said to him, “If your father could have had it, he would have paid a thousand horses for it.
sentences.n: The king is Sāsān; “his father” and “his uncle” are Kān Mā Kān's. kāna raʾāhu, “he had seen it”: kāna with a perfect makes a pluperfect, and the print keeps the precomposed hamza of رآه. min sanati kadhā wa-kadhā, “since the year such-and-such”, the storyteller's way of leaving a date vague. ʿabadat al-ṣulbān, “the worshippers of crosses”, the tale's standing name for the Byzantine Christians. The print runs law into qadara (لوقدر). qadara ʿalā, “to have power over, get hold of”. In law … la-ishtarāhu the lām marks the answer of the condition.

sentences.t: وَلٰكِنِ الْآنَ عَادَ الْعِزُّإِلَي أَهْلِهِ وَقَدْ قَبِلْنَاهُ وَمِنَّا لَكَ وَهَبْنَاهُ وَأَنْتَ أَحَقُّ بِهِ مِنْ كُلِّ إِنْسَانٍ لِأَنَّكَ سَيِّدُ الْفُرْسَانِ
sentences.tr: wa-lākini al-āna ʿāda al-ʿizzu ilā ahlihi wa-qad qabilnāhu wa-minnā laka wahabnāhu wa-anta aḥaqqu bihi min kulli insānin li-annaka sayyidu al-fursāni
sentences.l: But now the glory has-returned to its people; and we have accepted it, and from us to you we have-given-it; and you (are) more-entitled to it than every human-being, because you (are) the lord of the horsemen.
sentences.i: But now glory has come home to its rightful owners. We have accepted it, and now we make you a gift of it: you have a better right to it than any man alive, for you are the prince of horsemen.”
sentences.n: The print runs al-ʿizz into the following ilā (العزّالي), and writes ilā with a dotted yāʾ; the shadda on the zāy is printed. ʿāda al-ʿizzu ilā ahlihi, “glory has returned to its people”, a proverbial turn: the horse has come back where it belongs. Two rhymes run through the speech: qabilnāhu / wahabnāhu, then insān / fursān. minnā laka, “from us to you”, is put first for emphasis. aḥaqqu bi-, “having more right to”, with min for “than”. wa-lākini al-āna, “but now”: the light lākin, which needs no noun after it, takes a helping kasra before the article.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ أَمَرَ الْمَلِكُ سَاسَانُ أَنْ يُحْضِرُوا لِكَانَ مَا كَانَ الْخِلَعَ وَقَادَ لَهُ الْخُيُولَ
sentences.tr: thumma amara al-maliku sāsānu an yuḥḍirū li-kāna mā kāna al-khilaʿa wa-qāda lahu al-khuyūla
sentences.l: Then King Sāsān commanded that they bring to Kān Mā Kān the robes-of-honour, and he led to him the horses.
sentences.i: Then King Sāsān ordered robes of honour to be brought for Kān Mā Kān, and had horses led out for him as gifts.
sentences.n: khilaʿ, plural of khilʿa, a robe of honour given by a ruler as a mark of favour. amara an, “to order that”, with the subjunctive. li-kāna mā kāna: the preposition li- simply attaches to the name, which is itself a whole clause, “what was, was”. qāda, “to lead (a horse) by the bridle”; leading horses to someone is giving them to him.

sentences.t: وَأَفْرَدَ لَهُ فِى الْقَصْرِ أَكْبَرَ الدُّورِ وَأَقْبَلَ عَلَيْهِ الْعِزُّ وَالسُّرُورُ
sentences.tr: wa-afrada lahu fī al-qaṣri akbara al-dūri wa-aqbala ʿalayhi al-ʿizzu wa-al-surūru
sentences.l: And he set-apart for him in the palace the biggest of the dwellings; and there came-upon him the glory and the joy.
sentences.i: He gave him the largest apartments in the palace for his own, and honour and gladness came his way.
sentences.n: afrada li-, “to set aside for someone alone”. dūr, plural of dār, here the separate apartments of a palace. Rhyme: dūr, surūr. aqbala ʿalā, said of a person turning to someone (as when he turns to his mother just below), here of good fortune coming to meet him.

sentences.t: وَأَعْطَاهُ مَالًا جَزِيلًا وَأَكْرَمَهُ غَايَةَ الْإِكْرَامِ لِأَنَّهُ كَانَ يَخْشَى عَاقِبَةَ أَمْرِ الْوَزِيرِ دَنْدَانَ
sentences.tr: wa-aʿṭāhu mālan jazīlan wa-akramahu ghāyata al-ikrāmi li-annahu kāna yakhshā ʿāqibata amri al-wazīri dandāna
sentences.l: And he gave him abundant wealth, and honoured him the utmost of the honouring, because he was fearing the outcome of the affair of the vizier Dandān.
sentences.i: He gave him wealth in plenty and showed him every possible honour, for he feared where the vizier Dandān's doings might end.
sentences.n: ghāyata al-ikrām, “the limit of honouring”, an accusative of degree after its own verb, akrama. jazīl, “ample, abundant”, a stock companion of māl. kāna yakhshā, “he was fearing”: kāna with an imperfect gives a continuing state in the past. Sāsān has reason to court the boy: Dandān, the old vizier, has taken the army's loyalty away from him.

sentences.t: فَفَرِحَ بِذٰلِكَ كَانَ مَا كَانَ وَزَالَ عَنْهُ الذُّلُّ وَالْهَوَانُ
sentences.tr: fa-fariḥa bi-dhālika kāna mā kāna wa-zāla ʿanhu al-dhullu wa-al-hawānu
sentences.l: And Kān Mā Kān rejoiced at that, and there departed from him the abasement and the contempt.
sentences.i: Kān Mā Kān rejoiced at this, and the humiliation and contempt he had suffered fell away from him.
sentences.n: fariḥa bi-, “to be glad at”. zāla ʿan, “to pass away from, leave”. Rhyme: Kān Mā Kān, hawān. dhull and hawān are a stock pair, “abasement and scorn”.

sentences.t: وَدَخَلَ بَيْتَهُ وَأَقْبَلَ عَلَى أُمِّهِ وَقَالَ يَا أُمِّي كَيْفَ حَالُ ابْنَةِ عَمِّي
sentences.tr: wa-dakhala baytahu wa-aqbala ʿalā ummihi wa-qāla yā ummī kayfa ḥālu ibnati ʿammī
sentences.l: And he entered his house and turned to his mother and said: O my mother, how (is) the state of the daughter of my paternal-uncle?
sentences.i: He went into his house, turned to his mother and said, “Mother, how is my cousin?”
sentences.n: ibnat ʿammī, “my paternal uncle's daughter”, is the cousin a young man had the first claim to marry; here it is Qaḍā Fakān, Sharrukān's daughter. The alif of ibna is a joining alif and takes no hamza.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ وَاللَّهِ يَا وَلَدِي إِنَّ شُغْلِي بِغَيْبَتِكَ شَغَلَنِي عَنْ كُلِّ أَحَدٍ حَتَّي مَحْبُوبَتِكَ سِيَّمَا هِيَ كَانَتْ سَبَبًا لِغَيْبَتِكَ وَفُرْقَتِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat wa-allāhi yā waladī inna shughlī bi-ghaybatika shaghalanī ʿan kulli aḥadin ḥattā maḥbūbatika siyyamā hiya kānat sababan li-ghaybatika wa-furqatika
sentences.l: And she said: By God, O my son, my preoccupation with your absence occupied me from every one, even your beloved — especially (since) she was a cause of your absence and your separation.
sentences.i: She said, “By God, my son, I was so taken up with your absence that I gave no thought to anyone, not even your beloved — least of all her, since it was she who drove you away and parted you from us.”
sentences.n: shughlī … shaghalanī, “my occupation occupied me”, a figura etymologica: noun and verb from the same root. shaghala ʿan, “to distract from”. The print writes ḥattā with a dotted yāʾ (حتي). siyyamā without the usual lā (lā siyyamā, “especially”) is a common colloquial shortening; here it introduces a reason, “all the more since”. sabab li-, “a cause of”.

sentences.t: فَشَكَى إِلَيْهَا حَالَهُ وَقَالَ يَا أُمِّي امْضِي إِلَيْهَا وَأَقْبِلِي عَلَيْهَا لَعَلَّهَا تَجُودُ عَلَيَّ بِنَظْرَةٍ وَتُزِيلُ عَنِّي هٰذِهِ الْحَسْرَةَ
sentences.tr: fa-shakā ilayhā ḥālahu wa-qāla yā ummī imḍī ilayhā wa-aqbilī ʿalayhā laʿallahā tajūdu ʿalayya bi-naẓratin wa-tuzīlu ʿannī hādhihi al-ḥasrata
sentences.l: And he complained to her (of) his state, and said: O my mother, go to her and turn to her; perhaps she will be-generous to me with a glance and remove from me this anguish.
sentences.i: He poured out his trouble to her and said, “Mother, go to her and win her over; perhaps she will grant me one look and take this heartache from me.”
sentences.n: shakā ilā, “to complain to”, takes the trouble as a direct object: shakā ilayhā ḥālahu, “he laid his case before her”. The print spells the verb with alif maqṣūra (شكى) instead of the Classical شكا. imḍī and aqbilī are feminine imperatives, addressed to his mother. jāda ʿalā … bi-, “to be generous to someone with something”: the person takes ʿalā, the gift bi-. The print marks the shadda in laʿallahā and ʿalayya. Rhyme: naẓra, ḥasra.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لَهُ إِنَّ الْمَطَامِعَ تُذِلُّ رِقَابَ الرِّجَالِ فَدَعْ عَنْكَ مَا يُفْضِي إِلَى الْوَبَالِ فَإِنِّي لَا أَمْضِي إِلَيْهَا وَلَا أَدْخُلُ بِهٰذَا الْكَلَامِ عَلَيْهَا
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lahu inna al-maṭāmiʿa tudhillu riqāba al-rijāli fa-daʿ ʿanka mā yufḍī ilā al-wabāli fa-innī lā amḍī ilayhā wa-lā adkhulu bi-hādhā al-kalāmi ʿalayhā
sentences.l: And she said to him: Truly the cravings abase the necks of the men; so leave from you what leads to the ruin, for I will not go to her, nor go-in with this talk upon her.
sentences.i: She said to him, “Greed bows the necks of men; so put away from you what can only end in ruin. I will not go to her, nor carry such talk into her presence.”
sentences.n: A proverb in sajʿ: rijāl / wabāl, and then ilayhā / ʿalayhā. maṭāmiʿ, plural of maṭmaʿ, “object of desire, ambition”. adhalla, “to humble”; bending the neck is the posture of the abased. daʿ ʿanka, “let go of”, literally “leave (it) from you”. afḍā ilā, “to lead to, end in”. dakhala ʿalā bi-, “to go in to someone with” a message.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ مِنْ أُمِّهِ ذٰلِكَ أَخْبَرَهَا بِمَا قَالَهُ السَّلَّالُ مِنْ أَنَّ الْعَجُوزَ ذَاتَ الدَّوَاهِي طَرَقَتْ بِلَادَهُمْ وَقَصْدُهَا أَنْ تَدْخُلَ بَغْدَادَ وَهِيَ الَّتِي قَتَلَتْ عَمِّي وَجَدِّى وَلَا بُدَّ أَنِّي آخُذُ الثَّأْرَ وَأَكْشِفُ عَنَّا الْعَارَ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa min ummihi dhālika akhbarahā bi-mā qālahu al-sallālu min anna al-ʿajūza dhāta al-dawāhī ṭaraqat bilādahum wa-qaṣduhā an tadkhula baghdāda wa-hiya allatī qatalat ʿammī wa-jaddī wa-lā budda annī ākhudhu al-thaʾra wa-akshifu ʿannā al-ʿāra
sentences.l: And when he heard that from his mother, he told her what the horse-thief had said: that the old-woman Dhāt al-Dawāhī had come-by-night-into their lands and her aim (was) that she enter Baghdad — “and she (is) the one who killed my uncle and my grandfather, and there is no escape (but) that I take the blood-revenge and uncover from us the shame.”
sentences.i: When he heard this from his mother, he told her what the horse-thief had said: that the old woman Dhāt al-Dawāhī had stolen into their country, meaning to get into Baghdad. “It was she who killed my uncle and my grandfather,” he said, “and I must take vengeance for them and wipe this shame from us.”
sentences.n: ṭaraqa, “to come by night, knock at the door”, used of an unwelcome visitor. The report slides from reported speech (“their lands”) into Kān Mā Kān's own words (“my uncle and my grandfather”) without any qāla, a common move in the Nights. lā budda annī ākhudhu, “I must take”: Classical would say lā budda an ākhudha, with an and the subjunctive; here anna with a pronoun and the indicative. The print writes jaddī with alif maqṣūra (جدى) and leaves out the hamza of thaʾr (الثار); the precomposed hamza of آخذ is printed. Rhyme: thaʾr, ʿār. kashafa al-ʿār ʿan, “to lift the disgrace from”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ تَرَكَ أُمَّهُ وَأَقْبَلَ عَلَى عَجُوزٍ نَحْسٍ عَاهِرَةٍ مَاكِرَةٍ مُحْتَالَةٍ اسْمُهَا سَعْدَ انَةُ
sentences.tr: thumma taraka ummahu wa-aqbala ʿalā ʿajūzin naḥsin ʿāhiratin mākiratin muḥtālatin ismuhā saʿdānatu
sentences.l: Then he left his mother and turned to an old-woman, ill-omened, a whore, wily, tricky, her name (was) Saʿdāna.
sentences.i: Then he left his mother and went to an old woman, a jinx of a creature, a whore, sly and full of tricks, whose name was Saʿdāna.
sentences.n: The print sets the name as two words, سعد انة; it is one name, Saʿdāna, and the pointing here simply runs across the gap, so the two pieces are read together. naḥs, “bad luck, ill omen”, is a noun used here as an adjective, “a walking misfortune”. ʿāhira, “harlot”; mākira, “cunning”; muḥtāla, “a trickster”. The string of indefinite adjectives after ʿajūz is the storyteller's way of piling on abuse. The alif of ism is a joining alif and takes no hamza.

sentences.t: وَشَكَى إِلَيْهَا حَالَهُ وَمَا يَجِدُهُ مِنْ حُبِّ بِنْتِ عَمِّهِ قَضَى فَكَانَ وَسَأَلَهَا أَنْ تَمْضِيَ إِلَيْهَا وَتَسْتَعْطِفَهَا عَلَيْهِ فَقَالَتْ لَهُ الْعَجُوزُ السَّمْعُ وَالطَّاعَةُ
sentences.tr: wa-shakā ilayhā ḥālahu wa-mā yajiduhu min ḥubbi binti ʿammihi qaḍā fakāna wa-saʾalahā an tamḍiya ilayhā wa-tastaʿṭifahā ʿalayhi fa-qālat lahu al-ʿajūzu al-samʿu wa-al-ṭāʿatu
sentences.l: And he complained to her (of) his state and what he finds of love for the daughter of his paternal-uncle, Qaḍā Fakān, and he asked her that she go to her and make-her-tender toward him. And the old-woman said to him: The hearing and the obedience.
sentences.i: He laid his case before her, and told her what he suffered from love for his cousin Qaḍā Fakān, and asked her to go to the girl and soften her heart towards him. The old woman answered him, “With hearing and obedience.”
sentences.n: wajada, “to find”, is also “to feel”: mā yajiduhu min ḥubbi, “the love he feels”, with min explaining the mā. istaʿṭafa ʿalā, “to make someone feel tenderness toward”, the tenth form asking for ʿaṭf, “inclining, affection”. The print keeps the precomposed hamza of saʾalahā. al-samʿu wa-al-ṭāʿatu, the stock answer of a willing servant: nominatives, “(I owe you) hearing and obedience”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّهَا فَارَقَتْهُ وَذَهَبَتْ إِلَى قَصْرِ قَضَى فَكَانَ وَاسْتَعْطَفَتْ قَلْبَهَا عَلَيْهِ
sentences.tr: thumma innahā fāraqat-hu wa-dhahabat ilā qaṣri qaḍā fakāna wa-istaʿṭafat qalbahā ʿalayhi
sentences.l: Then she parted-from-him and went to the palace of Qaḍā Fakān, and made her heart tender toward him.
sentences.i: Then she left him and went to Qaḍā Fakān's palace, and set about winning her heart for him.
sentences.n: thumma innahā, “then she”: the storyteller's thumma inna before a fresh action. fāraqa, “to part from”, takes a direct object.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ عَادَتْ إِلَيْهِ وَأَعْلَمَتْهُ بِأَنَّ قَضَى فَكَانَ تُسَلِّمُ عَلَيْكَ وَوَعَدْتُهَا لَكَ أَنَّهَا فِي نِصْفِ اللَّيْلِ تَأْتِي إِلَيْكَ
sentences.tr: thumma ʿādat ilayhi wa-aʿlamat-hu bi-anna qaḍā fakāna tusallimu ʿalayka wa-waʿadtuhā laka annahā fī niṣfi al-layli taʾtī ilayka
sentences.l: Then she returned to him and informed him that Qaḍā Fakān greets you, and I have-made-an-appointment-with-her for you, that she at the half of the night comes to you.
sentences.i: Then she came back to him and told him, “Qaḍā Fakān sends you her greetings, and I have her promise for you: she will come to you at midnight.”
sentences.n: The sentence starts as reported speech (aʿlamat-hu bi-anna, “she informed him that”) and turns into the old woman's own words (“greets you”), as the Nights often does. sallama ʿalā, “to greet, send greetings to”. The print's وعدتها is unpointed and doubtful: read here as waʿadtuhā laka, “I have made an appointment with her for you”, which fits the old woman speaking; it could also be waʿadat-hā, “she promised it (the meeting)”. The precomposed hamza of taʾtī is printed.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَزَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the permitted speech.
sentences.i: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent, leaving the permitted speech.
